title: Will the ball swing round the peg? Halfway down: no, slack 48 deg short. 70 % down: yes. Needs 3/5
description:
Will the ball swing round the peg? A ball (a point mass) on a massless string of 1 m from a fixed pivot is let go from rest with the string horizontal, the ball level with the pivot on the left; a thin peg (zero radius) is fixed on the vertical below the pivot. Upper panel: the peg halfway down (0.5 m, so the ball turns on a circle of radius 0.5 m about the peg); lower panel: the peg 70 percent down (0.7 m, circle radius 0.3 m). Same ball, same swing, two pegs, on one clock; g = 9.80665 m/s^2; RK4 at 20,000 steps per second with the catch, the slack, the crossing of the vertical, the re-catch, the top and the laps located by bisection inside the step and checked against the closed forms; shown at 1/2.5 speed, the release repeating every 8.8 s of video, 5 releases in 44 s. When the string goes slack the ball flies as a projectile; while it is on the far side of the vertical the string is still round the peg and would snap taut if the ball's distance from the peg came back to 0.5 m; once it has crossed to the near side the string has slipped off the peg and runs straight from the pivot, snapping taut when the ball is 1 m from the pivot; the jerk kills the radial velocity and keeps the tangential part. Deterministic, no seed.

Measured:
- the swing down: the ball reaches the bottom at 0.5921 s (closed form sqrt(L / g) K(sin 45 deg) = 0.5921 s) at 4.4287 m/s (sqrt(2 g L) = 4.4287); the velocity there is horizontal, tangent to both circles, so the catch on the peg loses nothing; the string pull jumps from 3.0000 weights to 5.0000 weights (peg halfway) or 7.6667 weights (peg 70 % down)
- peg halfway down: the pull reaches 0 at 0.9408 s, 0.3487 s after the catch, at 131.81 degrees from the bottom about the peg = 48.19 degrees short of the top = 41.81 degrees above the peg's level (closed form cos psi = -2 (L - r) / (3 r) = -2/3), at 1.8080 m/s (sqrt(2 g (L - r) / 3)), 0.3333 m above the peg and 0.3727 m to the far side; the string goes slack and the ball flies: it peaks 0.4259 m above the peg 0.1374 s later, crosses the vertical 0.3092 s after the slack at 0.2813 m above the peg (0.2813 m from the peg, inside the 0.5 m circle, so the string round the peg never came taut) and is caught by the straight string 0.5608 s after the slack (1.5016 s after release), on the near side 17.65 degrees from the bottom about the pivot, moving at 4.3232 m/s 73.8 degrees below horizontal, almost straight along the string: the jerk kills 4.3218 m/s and keeps 0.1104 m/s, 0.062 percent of the bottom kinetic energy; afterwards the ball swings between 17.8 degrees left of the bottom about the pivot and 25.2 degrees right about the peg
- peg 70 percent down: the ball passes the top at 0.8562 s, 0.2641 s after the catch, at 2.8009 m/s (sqrt(2 g L - 4 g r) = 2.8009; it needs sqrt(g r) = 1.7152) with the pull 1.6667 weights (2 L / r - 5), the minimum over the laps; the string stays taut and the ball loops the peg; every lap takes 0.5283 s (spread 9.2e-14 s; quadrature of r dpsi / v over 2 pi = 0.5283 s), 6 laps in the 4 s run
- the threshold: the string is taut at the top only if 2 g L - 4 g r is at least g r, i.e. r is at most 2 L / 5, so the peg must be at least 3 L / 5 = 0.60 m down; peg 0.59 L: does not loop, the pull reaches 0 at 163.61 degrees from the bottom (16.39 short of the top), the top would need v^2 = 4.0207 against 3.5304 available; peg 0.60 L: the string just reaches the top with zero pull (4.34e-09 weights, top speed 1.9806 m/s = sqrt(g r)); peg 0.61 L: loops, 2.0772 m/s over the top (needs 1.9557) with the pull 0.1282 weights
- RK4 stays within 3.5e-14 weights (upper) and 7.6e-14 weights (lower) of the energy closed form for the pull, and within 2.0e-15 s of the elliptic quarter period for the time to the bottom

Why: the ball keeps the same energy whichever peg it meets, so at any height it has the same speed on either circle. What the peg changes is the size of the circle. To stay on a circle the string has to pull the ball inward with v^2 / r, minus what gravity already supplies; at the top gravity supplies exactly g, so the string is taut there only if v_top^2 is at least g r. The top of the small circle sits 2 r above the bottom, so v_top^2 = 2 g L - 4 g r, and the condition that 2 g L - 4 g r is at least g r gives r at most 2 L / 5: the peg must be at least three fifths of the way down. Halfway down (r = L / 2) the ball would arrive at the top with v^2 = 0, and it never gets there: the pull hits zero 48 degrees short of the top, the string goes slack, the ball flies on a parabola inside the circle and drops onto the string. Seventy percent down (r = 0.3 L) it passes the top at 2.8 m/s with 1.67 weights of pull to spare and loops the peg lap after lap.
